/-!
# Erdős Problem 1094

*Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/1094](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1094)
-/

@[expose] public section

namespace Erdos1094

open scoped Nat

/--
For all $n\ge 2k$ the least prime factor of $\binom{n}{k}$ is $\le\max(n/k,k)$, with only
finitely many exceptions.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_1094 :
    {(n, k) : ℕ × ℕ | 0 < k ∧ 2 * k ≤ n ∧ (n.choose k).minFac > max (n / k) k}.Finite := by
  sorry

end Erdos1094

reformulations.difference: The source says: for n ≥ 2k, the least prime factor of C(n,k) is ≤ max(n/k, k), with finitely many exceptions (n/k is the real ratio). The Lean differs in form in three ways. (1) It writes the bound as `max (n / k) k` using ℕ floor division. (2) It takes the least prime factor to be `Nat.minFac`. (3) It adds the domain restriction `0 < k`, and states 'finitely many exceptions' as `Set.Finite` of the set of exceptional pairs (n, k) : ℕ × ℕ.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: (1) Floor division. For natural p and k > 0: p > ⌊n/k⌋ ⟺ n < p·k (`Nat.div_lt_iff_lt_mul`) ⟺ (n:ℝ)/k < p (`div_lt_iff₀`). After splitting with `max_lt_iff`, `minFac > max (n / k) k` is equivalent to the real-division condition, so the two exception sets are equal. I proved `set_eq_real` (set equality) and `stmt_iff_real` (the finiteness statements are equivalent) in a scratch file. (2) minFac. On the domain 0 < k, 2k ≤ n we have C(n,k) ≥ 2, from `Nat.choose_pos` and `Nat.choose_eq_one_iff` (proved). So `Nat.minFac` is a prime dividing C(n,k) and is ≤ every prime divisor (proved). It is exactly the least prime factor. (3) `0 < k`. The source's k is implicitly ≥ 1: C(n,0) = 1 has no prime factor, and n/0 is meaningless. Without this hypothesis every (n, 0) would count as an exception, since minFac 1 = 1 > max (n/0) 0 = 0 (checked in Lean). Also k = 1 never gives an exception (checked), so whether the source means k ≥ 1 or k ≥ 2 makes no difference. Counting exceptions as pairs or as binomial values is equivalent, because each value arises from finitely many pairs (C(n,k) ≥ n). Sanity check: evaluating the exact Lean predicate for n ≤ 1200 gives exactly the 14 exceptions listed in ELS88 and on erdosproblems.com: (7,3), (13,4), (14,4), (23,5), (44,8), (46,10), (47,10), (47,11), (62,6), (74,10), (94,10), (95,10), (241,16), (284,28).

review.notes:
The file has one declaration, `Erdos1094.erdos_1094`. It states the problem exactly as erdosproblems.com poses it: "For all n ≥ 2k the least prime factor of C(n,k) is ≤ max(n/k, k), with only finitely many exceptions." Its docstring repeats that sentence word for word.

The recorded category, `research open`, matches the source. The problem page (archived 2026-07-09) says "OPEN — This is open, and cannot be resolved with a finite computation", and the community database also records it as open.

The quantifier structure is right: a finite set of exceptional pairs, with the domain 0 < k and 2k ≤ n. The inequality direction is right: an exception means minFac > max. Using ℕ floor division is equivalent to the source's real n/k, and I proved this in Lean (see reformulations).

Evaluating the exact Lean predicate for n ≤ 1200 gives exactly the 14 exceptions that ELS88 and the site list. The statement is neither trivially true nor trivially false.

ELS88 poses a sharper claim: exactly those 14 exceptions. There are also stronger variants: max(n/k, √k), max(n/k, O(log k)), and ELS93's max(n/k, 13) with 12 exceptions. The file includes none of these as variants. That is an omission, not a misformalization, because the main statement matches the problem as posed.

I could not read ELS93 (Math. Comp. 61 (1993) 215–224) because the AMS site is behind Cloudflare. It is not needed for the statement under review.
